title: Day-ahead net load forecasting in ZEBs: A comparative ML study with novel feature engineering and simulation-based evaluation
abstract: The growing deployment of zero-energy buildings supports the transition toward a more sustainable building stock. In practice, many of these buildings operate under behind-the-meter configurations to reduce infrastructure costs and simplify data management. However, this monitoring approach constrains the effective exploitation of their flexibility potential, as forecasting shifts from load to net load and must account for the combined uncertainty of demand and photovoltaic generation. To address this challenge, we systematically benchmark a broad range of classical machine-learning and state-of-the-art deep-learning models within a forecasting pipeline that directly predicts the net load profile of a zero-energy building. We further propose a joint hyperparameter and feature selection optimisation framework that integrates model-based feature importance with greedy forward feature addition inside a Bayesian optimisation procedure. Model performance is evaluated using conventional forecasting metrics as well as newly introduced domain-informed measures designed to assess peak and valley prediction accuracy. To reflect the ultimate objective of flexibility provision, we also embed the forecasts in a simulation-based battery dispatch framework that enhances photovoltaic self-consumption and provides peak-shaving support to a distribution transformer. Results show that although several models achieve strong statistical accuracy, XGBoost delivers superior operational performance in the simulation-based evaluation, an advantage not fully reflected by statistical error metrics. The proposed domain-informed metrics, however, successfully identify LightGBM as a consistently strong alternative in capturing operationally relevant dynamics. A sensitivity analysis across different battery capacities further reveals that the selection of forecasting model has a limited impact at low storage levels, where outcomes remain comparable, but becomes increasingly critical as storage capacity grows, significantly influencing planning and flexibility provision.

title: Quantifying provincial contributions to carbon intensity reduction in China’s construction industry: ML-assisted analysis via an integrated LMDI-ANCOVA framework
abstract: A clear understanding of the drivers of carbon intensity in China’s construction industry is essential for tracking progress toward emission reduction targets. We first use the traditional logarithmic mean Divisia index (LMDI) method to quantify the contributions of 30 mainland provinces and their related economic variables to the decline in construction carbon intensity from 2006 to 2020. We then adopt machine learning-assisted analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with K-means clustering as the specific machine learning technique, to quantify the effect size of driving variables. This two-step framework integrates LMDI decomposition results with statistical validation, avoiding bias from single-method analysis. Results show that provincial changes in carbon intensity, energy intensity, energy structure, output value share, and emission share jointly shape the national trend, with the eastern and northeastern regions as the main contributors. Three paradoxical phenomena are identified: (1) large provincial declines may have limited national impact when economic weight is small (Xinjiang), (2) local emission reductions may be offset by rapid economic expansion (Fujian, Shaanxi), and (3) industrial contraction may mask efficiency improvements (Liaoning). Full-chain energy intensity and provincial carbon intensity management are the dominant drivers of reduction, while the carbon reduction potential of the energy structure is relatively large. Zhejiang and Jilin made outstanding contributions, whereas several provinces restrained national progress. This study integrates provincial and national carbon intensity indicators into a unified framework, providing robust evidence for differentiated, region-specific policies to achieve China’s construction industry carbon reduction goals.

title: Cleanroom environmental control systems: review of research landscape and control strategies
abstract: • Identify the overarching research landscape for energy efficiency in cleanrooms. • Summarize the control variables, objectives, control methods for cleanrooms. • Propose future directions for advanced controls, integrating AI technologies. • Airflow and contamination dominate studies; optimization and efficiency are rising. • Ventilation control is most common; air change rate is the key control variable. Cleanroom is an emerging and high-energy–density building type. The heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) systems of cleanrooms can consume up to 100 times more energy than those used in commercial spaces of the same size. This study presents a systematic literature review on the overall research landscape of HVAC systems in cleanrooms, analyzing trends, advances, and gaps in this area of research. In addition, the review provides an in-depth analysis of control strategies for cleanroom HVAC systems. A comprehensive examination of 235 papers was conducted to provide an overarching research landscape, with 55 papers specifically focused on control strategies selected for an in-depth review. The analysis reveals that contamination control consistently emerges as the predominant research topic in the field, while optimization and energy efficiency have gained increasing prominence in recent years, as evidenced by keyword evolution mapping. Semiconductor cleanrooms received more research attention compared to other cleanroom applications. Among the various control strategies utilized in cleanroom HVAC systems, ventilation controls are the most widely studied, with air change rate serving as the most frequent control variable. Ventilation controls, such as demand flow control, exhibit a higher energy saving rate. Cleanroom control strategies remain highly conservative, with the majority utilizing rule-based control, and only 23.6% of studies focusing on optimization-based approaches. Nearly half of the reviewed control-related works incorporated experimental evaluations to validate their proposed control methods. The application of advanced technologies in cleanrooms is still limited. Future research directions could emphasize investigating the potential of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and big data analytics to improve cleanroom performance and control.

title: Modeling occupant air-conditioning behavior in mediterranean offices with manual HVAC control: A case study conducted in montpellier during summer 2025
abstract: Occupant behavior related to air conditioning (AC) has a considerable impact on the energy consumption of office buildings, particularly in southern France, which is characterized by a hot Mediterranean climate and frequent heat waves. Although several studies have developed behavioral models using logistic regression, relatively few have examined the application of machine learning methods to predict occupant behavior in French offices during the summer months. To address this gap, this paper presents a comparative study of four modeling approaches for predicting AC activation behavior: logistic regression, random forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and support vector machines. The research is an exploratory, case-study-based investigation carried out in Montpellier during the summer of 2025 (June to September) in six offices occupied by 14 individuals. Models were trained per office using datasets including 1270 to 3039 AC on/off observations, with class distributions ranging from 24-65% for the "on" status and 35-76% for the "off" status. Five distinct occupant profiles were identified based on AC usage patterns. The highest F1score achieved was 0.65, obtained with both logistic regression and random forest in an office with a single, consistent usage pattern. Lower performance was observed in offices with diverse behaviors and class imbalance. Compared with prior literature reporting F1-scores above 0.8, these results highlight the challenges of modeling AC behavior in small-scale, diverse office environments. Overall, the findings show that model transferability is limited across different offices and that feature importance varies across algorithms, emphasizing the need for tailored, contextspecific modeling approaches to predict AC activation behavior.

title: A large language model-driven automated workflow for CFD simulations of urban street canyons
Publicly accessible data and computer vision for retrofit planning: Evidence from London social housing
abstract: Buildings account for approximately 34% of global CO₂ emissions, placing the built environment at the centre of climate action. Aging social housing represents a particularly under-studied challenge: in the United Kingdom, around 78% of the building stock predates 1980, and nearly 60% of buildings carry poor energy performance ratings. Systematic retrofit planning is further hampered by building data that is incomplete and fragmented across disparate sources. This paper presents a pilot study investigating data-driven approaches to support social housing retrofit planning across several London boroughs. Using publicly accessible property datasets, computer vision training data, and street-level imagery, we fine-tuned convolutional neural networks to predict two retrofit-relevant building characteristics: wall construction type and architectural style. In-distribution accuracy reached up to 94%; however, performance declined substantially when models were evaluated against property samples provided by local councils. This highlights the generalisation challenges inherent in applying models trained on publicly accessible data to real-world contexts, and underscores the need for broader, purpose-built labelled datasets. A stakeholder workshop with representatives from local government, retrofit organisations, and industry consultancies complemented the technical findings. Discussions surfaced practical barriers to data use in the retrofit sector, including inconsistent data formats, limited inter-organisational data sharing, and a lack of coordination across the supply chain. The findings suggest that publicly accessible housing data and machine learning hold genuine promise for large-scale urban retrofit characterisation, but that realising this potential will require greater data standardisation, coordinated investment in labelled datasets, and closer collaboration across the sector.

title: Predicting after-renovation value to support investment decisions: A data-driven approach
abstract: The European building stock is highly energy inefficient, highlighting the need for effective incentives to accelerate energy efficiency renovations. Beyond reducing energy consumption, such refurbishments can generate additional benefits, including increases in property value, which are particularly relevant for homeowners and investors. Thus, quantifying the relationship between energy performance and after-renovation property value is essential for supporting investment decisions and capturing the broader economic impact of renovation. This study proposes a data-driven decision-support framework to estimate residential property prices and predict the market value effects of energy efficiency upgrades. Using a large dataset of approximately 270,000 residential listings from Greece, a gradient boosting model is developed, incorporating structural, spatial, and energy performance features. The model achieves strong predictive performance, with an R 2 score of 0.86 on the test set. It is subsequently employed to perform counterfactual simulations of energy performance certificate improvements, enabling the estimation of expected price changes following a renovation. The results indicate a positive relationship between energy performance and property value, with substantial improvements in energy performance certificate ratings associated with price increases of up to 30%. A replication study using Austrian residential market data yields comparable accuracy, demonstrating the robustness of the approach across different European markets. Overall, the proposed approach provides a transparent and scalable data-driven framework for quantifying the economic benefits of energy efficiency renovations, supporting decision-making for homeowners, investors and policy makers.

title: A hybrid deep learning–ensemble model for accurate and explainable electricity demand forecasting in renewable energy communities
abstract: Accurate, interpretable, and scalable short-term electricity demand forecasting is a crucial requirement for transitioning towards decentralized, citizen-driven energy systems, particularly within renewable energy communities (RECs). The proposed framework utilizes long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) to capture both the sequential dynamics of consumption and the nonlinear interactions between household and community-level characteristics. A stratified household selection strategy based on contribution-level binning is employed to ensure coverage across distinct demand regimes while maintaining computational efficiency. Based on 15-minute smart meter data from a renewable energy community in Loureiro, Portugal, the hybrid model achieved the lowest prediction errors at both scales, with a best-case household-level mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 1.25% and a community-level average MAPE of 3.14%, corresponding to explained variance ( R 2 ) values of 0.9420 and 0.9558, respectively. Although XGBoost performed slightly better for specific low-variability households, the hybrid approach consistently outperformed the standalone models in terms of accuracy and robustness. The model’s interpretation is enhanced by SHAP, which reveals distinct demand drivers for consumers, including memory-based characteristics and climatic variables like temperature and solar radiation. The Interpretive, multi-level Prediction framework provides a reliable basis for practical REC applications, such as battery planning, peer-to-peer trading, and real-time demand response.

title: The evolution of inverse optimization: A cross-disciplinary review of algorithmic approaches and application framework in building life cycle assessment
abstract: Optimization techniques have become fundamental tools for addressing complex decision making challenges across diverse domains, yet traditional forward optimization approaches often struggle with incomplete information, unknown preferences, and dynamic constraints. This literature review examines the emerging field of inverse optimization as a complementary paradigm that works backward from observed solutions to infer underlying objectives and constraints. While forward optimization has been extensively applied in building design and life cycle assessment, it faces limitations in early design stages where 20% of decisions determine 80% of future performance outcomes. This review synthesizes 95 studies across seven disciplines and 69 within the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction industry to analyze how inverse optimization enhances sustainable building design. Results show rapid growth of applications after 2020, led by China, the U.S., and the U.K., with 58% of studies targeting environmental performance, 43% economic, and 10% social factors. Hybrid and machine-learning-based inverse methods, particularly genetic algorithms, neural networks, and Gaussian processes dominate recent research, enabling improved model calibration, faster convergence, and robustness under uncertainty. Inverse optimization is found effective in extracting decision logic from empirical data, calibrating energy models, and managing multi-objective trade-offs between energy, comfort, and cost. Despite these advances, methodological gaps remain such as the lack of standardized inverse Life Cycle Assessment workflows, limited coupling between inverse models and Building Information Modeling platforms, and insufficient methods for handling uncertainty and multi-objective trade-offs in early-stage design. Building on this synthesis and on prior methodological reviews in operations research, the review proposes a framework integrating Inverse Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), multi-objective decision-making, and LCA to guide data driven, adaptive approaches for optimizing environmental performance in buildings.

title: Bridging the heating equity gap in income-based energy burden metrics: A feature-based framework for identifying thermally vulnerable households
abstract: Traditional income-based energy poverty metrics often fail to identify vulnerable households that deliberately limit their energy use to reduce financial strain, potentially falling under energy poverty thresholds at the cost of unsafe thermal conditions. Failure to detect these thermally vulnerable households creates a heating equity gap —defined as the shortfall between medically-grounded World Health Organization thresholds recommended for healthy adults and indoor temperatures—causes vulnerable households to remain unidentified as energy poor, thus rendering them ineligible for support programs while exposing them to serious health risks. To address this gap, we introduce an explainable AI-driven dual vulnerability assessment framework that integrates indoor temperature-based thermal vulnerability with heating activation behavior to improve cross-context comparability and minimize misclassifications caused by biased thresholds. Analysis employing a synthetically generated dataset of N=6,000 households, created through statistical augmentation of population-level energy consumption and housing characteristic distributions calibrated to Montana’s climate region during winter months, has identified 713 thermally vulnerable households (11.9%), of which 91.2% and 50.4% were overlooked by the standard 10% and 2M energy burden thresholds, respectively. Feature importance analysis shows that the strongest vulnerability predictors are energy consumption patterns, income level, and behavioral inflection temperatures. Interaction effects further reveal that building characteristics and economic constraints impact vulnerability in ways not captured by single factors: 18% of households maintain adequate indoor temperatures despite delayed heating activation, whereas 10% experience thermal vulnerability despite normal heating activation patterns. By distinguishing households that require structural improvements from those that need immediate financial assistance, this explainable framework provides actionable guidance to policymakers. It fundamentally shifts energy poverty assessment toward a multidimensional perspective—one that integrates socioeconomic factors, actual thermal conditions, structural housing characteristics, and behavioral adaptations to capture hidden forms of energy insecurity.

title: An adaptive building energy anomaly detection and load prediction framework with factorized sequential neural networks
Identifying residential building energy retrofit priorities across climate zones and end uses using machine learning and explainable AI
abstract: Energy retrofits of existing residential buildings are essential for reducing energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. However, limited resources require effective prioritization of retrofit measures. As retrofit effectiveness varies by climate zones, end uses, building characteristics, and future climate conditions, uniform retrofit strategies are often inefficient at national scales. Unlike previous studies that typically focus on a single climate condition or energy end use, this study develops a data-driven framework systematically comparing climate-zone and end-use-specific retrofit priorities under both historical and future climate scenarios, enabling climate-responsive retrofit planning and policy development. A synthetic database of over 72,000 parametric simulations of residential building archetypes is used to train climate-zone-specific machine learning (ML) models for predicting heating and cooling energy use intensity (EUI). Explainable artificial intelligence, based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), is applied to interpret model predictions and quantify parameter importance and directional influence. Results show substantial climate-zone-dependent differences in retrofit priorities. For cooling EUI, window SHGC and south-facing façade window-to-wall ratio (FDWR) are the two most influential features across all climate zones, exhibiting SHAP distributions approximately 1.5–2 times wider than those of other features. Cooling system efficiency and foundation type are additional key retrofit priorities in warmer and transitional climates (CZ 4–6), whereas ventilation rate plays a larger role in colder zones (CZ 7 A–8). For heating EUI, window U-value dominates in CZ 4–5, with SHAP ranges approximately 2–3 times wider than other variables, while foundation type becomes the primary driver in CZ 6–8. Under future climate scenarios, mechanical cooling efficiency gains importance in CZ 4-7 A, while heating performance in colder zones remains dominated by envelope, foundation, and ventilation system with heat recovery. Overall, the proposed ML-XAI framework provides transparent insights to support regionally differentiated climate-responsive retrofit strategies and evidence-based energy policy development.

title: Development of a statistical model for long-term electricity forecasting in residential buildings
abstract: Buildings account for 36–40% of global energy consumption and CO₂ emissions, with electricity representing nearly 55% of global electricity use. Accurate long-term forecasting is critical for grid stability and net-zero targets, yet most predictive models require extensive multi-year datasets or complex machine learning architectures. To our knowledge, no prior study has employed Fourier series methods integrating climate variables and weekday residual corrections to predict full annual electricity consumption using only a single year of training data, representing a methodological gap for long-term, one-year-ahead prediction in data-scarce environments. This study develops a simple modeling framework using Fourier series enhanced by multivariate regression incorporating climate variables (air temperature, humidity, sunshine hours) and seasonal residual correction. The developed models were tested on 322 apartments in a residential building in Japan, using hierarchical clustering to identify distinct consumption clusters (low, medium and high). The model achieved high accuracy across all clusters in this case study (RMSE = 0.472–1.20 kWh, MAPE = 7.1–8.9%) when forecasting one year ahead. Autoregressive residual correction further improved day-ahead forecasting accuracy (RMSE = 0.49–0.83 kWh, MAPE = 4.8–5.5%). Residual analysis revealed systematic weekday–weekend patterns and strong correlations with temperature. High-consumption clusters exhibited two to three times greater temperature sensitivity than low-consumption groups. The proposed Fourier approach provides an interpretable, data-efficient alternative to complex machine learning models, enabling accurate one-year-ahead electricity forecasting using only a single year of historical data. It offers a practical tool for building energy managers and policymakers operating in data-constrained contexts.

title: Measured heating impacts of window retrofits in cold, dry-winter housing: Changepoint diagnostics with AI-assisted interpretation
abstract: Window retrofits are widely implemented in existing residential buildings, yet their measured heating impacts under real operating conditions remain insufficiently verified, particularly in cold-climate regions with high seasonal heating demand. This study evaluates the measured heating impacts of a government-supported window retrofit program in cold, dry-winter housing using pre- and post-retrofit utility data from 39 dwellings in Goyang City, South Korea. A three-parameter heating changepoint model (3PH-CPM) was used to derive temperature-adjusted heating diagnostics, including heating slope, heating-zone intercept, base load, and heating energy above base. Retrofit effects were then assessed through parametric and nonparametric pre-post statistical tests. The results showed statistically significant post-retrofit improvements in key heating diagnostics, indicating reduced temperature sensitivity and lower heating demand. To examine heterogeneity in retrofit response, dwellings were grouped using CPM-derived heating metrics reflecting improvement magnitude, heating sensitivity, and pre-retrofit energy use. AI-assisted interpretation based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was then applied to identify the household and building characteristics associated with stronger or weaker measured benefits. The analysis revealed both the magnitude and direction of variable influence, highlighting the physical and occupancy-related factors linked to heterogeneous retrofit outcomes. The proposed dual-level evaluation framework provides a transparent and practical approach for assessing measured window retrofit performance under weather-varying conditions and may support more informed screening and follow-up evaluation of retrofit programs in heating-dominated regions.

title: Extension-layer fine-tuning for transfer learning in multi-agent reinforcement learning-based HVAC control
abstract: Reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) control, but its practical application is limited by high training costs and insufficient cross-environment generalization. Although existing transfer learning methods can partly alleviate this issue, their transfer stability and adaptability remain limited in complex HVAC systems involving multi-agent interactions. To address this challenge, this study develops an extension-layer fine-tuning strategy within the multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) framework for transferring multifunctional HVAC control policies, where separate agents regulate indoor temperature setpoints and fresh-air ventilation. During transfer, the pretrained actor and critic networks are retained as transferable knowledge backbones, and newly added adaptation layers are trained to capture target-environment-specific policy and value-function representations. The proposed strategy is compared with partial fine-tuning, full-model fine-tuning, MADDPG trained from scratch, and a rule-based controller under cross-climate and cross-building-type transfer scenarios. The results show that, across all test scenarios, the proposed strategy maintains indoor temperature and CO2 concentration within prescribed ranges while achieving energy-saving performance comparable to fully trained MADDPG. In addition, compared with training from scratch, transfer learning reduces retraining time by more than 90%, and the additional computational burden introduced by the newly added adaptation layers is limited. These results indicate that extension-layer fine-tuning provides an effective pathway for efficiently and reliably deploying multi-agent reinforcement learning controllers in heterogeneous building environments.

title: Multi-objective optimization of sinusoidal impinging jet ventilation under medium-to-high cooling loads using a hybrid CFD-machine learning approach
Physics-informed RC–MLP modelling for building thermal prediction
abstract: Reliable multi-horizon building thermal prediction is essential for energy-efficient HVAC operation, model predictive control, and demand response, yet existing models often face trade-offs among physical interpretability, data efficiency, and predictive accuracy. This study develops a physics-informed RC–MLP modelling framework for single-zone indoor temperature prediction using a publicly available high-resolution operational dataset from real office spaces. A 4R3C resistance–capacitance model was first selected as the grey-box thermal baseline by comparing candidate RC structures using both prediction accuracy and physical parameter plausibility. A residual multi-layer perceptron was then trained to correct systematic RC prediction errors using horizon-specific features derived from thermal history, solar forcing, time-of-day variables, and operational indicators. The framework was evaluated at prediction horizons of 5, 30, 60, 180, and 360 min under standard, seasonal shift, and limited-data conditions. Results show that prediction accuracy alone was insufficient for RC structure selection, as candidate models produced similar RMSE values while only the 4R3C structure satisfied all plausibility checks. Residual analysis revealed autocorrelated, diurnal, and solar-driven error structures. On the standard split, the RC–MLP model reduced RMSE by 4.4% at 30 min and 21.3% at 360 min relative to the RC baseline. Under seasonal shift, it retained a 16.8% improvement at 360 min, whereas limited-data experiments showed that mismatched residual calibration could degrade performance. These findings demonstrate that physically plausible RC models provide robust baseline predictions, while residual MLP correction is most effective when calibration data are representative of deployment conditions.

title: Scalable HVAC flexibility aggregation with DRL and linear programming
abstract: Large-scale HVAC demand response can provide grid flexibility, but market participation requires fast aggregate allocation, device-level feasibility and protection of occupant comfort. Although recent research has advanced building-flexibility assessment, learning-based control and distributed service provision, evidence is still limited for allocating a post-clearing dispatch request across many lower-level HVAC aggregators while accounting for accumulated thermal comfort burden. Here we develop a hierarchical aggregation framework in which a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) allocator assigns market-requested flexibility among resource aggregators using both current conditions and accumulated comfort impact. Local linear programming (LP) controllers then schedule HVAC operation under comfort and power constraints. The framework is evaluated for supply-demand adjustment requests defined by flexibility magnitude, direction, response-time tolerance and continuous delivery period. Compared with a centralised LP benchmark and a rule-based Greedy+LP baseline, the proposed DRL+LP framework reduces computation from more than 1,000 to a few seconds at large scale. At the 3,600-room scale, it assigns requests up to 0.792 MW for three hours and keeps aggregate assigned requests within a ± 10% tolerance in nearly all reported extraction intervals. Its comfort-violation metrics remain close to the centralised LP reference, with absolute differences no larger than 0.052 ∘ C in mean absolute error (MAE) and 0.045 ∘ C 2 in mean squared error (MSE) in the reported cases. It also avoids the uneven comfort burden observed in greedy allocation under low-flexibility requests. In an unseen two-request daily scenario, the learned policy maintains request allocation within tolerance and median comfort deviations of approximately 0.04–0.05 ∘ C. These results establish a scalable and comfort-aware allocation approach within the simulated market-dispatch and continuously modulatable HVAC setting considered here. Evidence remains limited to a single calibrated room model, cooling operation and one climatic region; performance under heating, heterogeneous buildings, diverse occupancy and field communication or model uncertainty has not yet been established.

title: Soft state-of-charge estimation for adsorption energy storage: Black-box and physics-informed approaches
abstract: Adsorption-based thermochemical energy storage is an emerging technology with strong potential for waste-heat recovery and integration into sector-coupled energy systems. However, operating such complex systems remains challenging and requires in-depth data analysis. One of the key challenges is the real-time, precise tracking of State-of-Charge (SOC) instead of relying on temperature difference in the external adsorption and desorption loops. In this context, this work develops and validates machine learning models as soft sensors of the key states in adsorption-based thermal energy storage systems, overcoming the real-time limitations of conventional physics-based approaches. Using experimental data collected through an edge computing platform, we evaluate both black-box Neural Networks (NNs) and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). The goal of using instantaneous sensor data is to reconstruct (estimate) the unmeasurable current states, mainly the refrigerant update and the adsorption-desorption temperatures in real-time. The proposed PINN introduces a specialized physical loss coupling thermochemical energy balances with adsorption kinetics, driven by instantaneous edge inputs for direct SoC tracking. The comparative evaluation demonstrates that PINN consistently achieves higher predictive accuracy than the conventional NN across all key outputs, relative to a high-fidelity white-box dynamic model. For the adsorption and desorption mass fractions, the PINN attains R 2 values of 0.939 and 0.938, respectively, improving upon the NN's 0.922 and 0.905. Similarly, for adsorption and desorption temperature estimations, the PINN achieves R 2 values of 0.994 and 0.992 compared to the NN's 0.989 and 0.985. These improvements correspond to 15–25% reductions in MSE, MAE, and RMSE, confirming a more precise reconstruction of key thermodynamic states. When applied to SOC estimation, the PINN further demonstrates enhanced fidelity with R 2 value of 0.939 versus 0.922 for the NN, highlighting its ability to generalize the coupled adsorption-desorption behavior by integrating the system's thermochemical energy balance and driving force relationships into the learning process. A robustness test with noisy measurements, reflecting real-world industrial conditions, confirmed that the PINN outperforms the standard NN due to its embedded physical constraints.

title: Multi-agent storage dispatch in building communities: Information availability, inter-building dynamics, and the distribution of benefits
abstract: Building energy communities are expected to provide grid flexibility through coordinated storage dispatch, and multi-agent reinforcement learning is increasingly proposed to deliver it. This study evaluates, on one CityLearn benchmark instance, the relative value of temporal representation under a pre-specified removal of weather and solar lead variables, and asks how the benefits of dispatch are distributed across a community. A five-building community from the CityLearn 2020 Climate Zone 1 benchmark is used to evaluate multi-agent proximal policy optimisation under centralised training with decentralised execution. A pre-registered 2 × 3 factorial crosses temporal representation against the availability of forecast information over five paired seeds and full-year episodes, alongside three reference controllers this literature rarely reports together: a rule-based schedule, a zero-action null controller, and a rolling-horizon model predictive controller with stated information assumptions. Withholding weather and solar leads did not differentially advantage the temporal controller over a capacity-matched feed-forward one: the paired difference-in-differences interval lies inside a pre-specified ± 2% equivalence bound. Under perfect foresight, model predictive control is cheaper than every learned controller, and the null controller records the lowest ramping cost of any controller evaluated, so ramping improvements measured only against a rule-based baseline may reflect that baseline’s own storage activity. Contribution to district peaks does not follow energy share: one building’s share of peak-hour load is 2.18 times its share of annual energy, an ordering unchanged by a controller that dispatches nothing. Two limits of the benchmark are reported as results. Comfort is exactly invariant across all controllers, because storage cannot actuate indoor temperature; and same-building warming cannot be simulated, because demand and indoor series are precomputed.

title: Climate-adaptive thermal performance assessment of naturally ventilated offices using surrogate modeling under present and future climates
abstract: Building performance assessment under climate change requires surrogate models capable of representing diverse climatic conditions while remaining computationally efficient. However, representing weather information in surrogate models is challenging because climate variables consist of long, highly variable time series that cannot be directly used as model inputs. This study develops and evaluates a surrogate-modeling framework for rapid overheating assessment in naturally ventilated cellular office buildings using compact climatic descriptors. More than 155,000 EnergyPlus simulations were performed using historical and future weather files, and twelve alternative approaches for representing wind speed and direction were systematically evaluated. Artificial neural networks were trained to predict the fraction of occupied hours with operative temperatures above 26~°C (FHOT26). The selected surrogate model achieved high predictive accuracy (R² = 0.949, MAE = 0.037, AE95 = 0.157). The results show that predictive performance depends not only on the climatic variables adopted but also on how they are represented. The highest accuracy was obtained by combining occupancy-hour descriptors for wind direction with full-day descriptors for wind speed, indicating that climatic variables should be represented according to the physical mechanisms through which they influence building performance. Training exclusively with historical weather data did not compromise predictive performance under future climate scenarios, and the model also generalized well to geographically distinct climates. The proposed framework provides an efficient and transferable methodology for incorporating climatic information into surrogate models, supporting rapid climate-adaptive overheating assessment during early-stage building design.

title: Building energy prediction under future climate scenarios: A Hybrid multi-scale graph–temporal framework with physics-based corrections
abstract: Global warming is causing future climate conditions to gradually deviate from historical distributions. This shift introduces considerable uncertainty into power distribution planning, energy efficiency retrofits, and load management in buildings. Existing studies have not fully considered the input features related to multi-scale fluctuations in building load series. In addition, many previous methods remain tied to the historical distribution of building energy consumption, which limits their direct applicability to non-stationary load responses under future climate conditions. Therefore, predicting building energy consumption under such scenarios remains insufficiently addressed. To reduce the instability caused by directly training graph–temporal neural networks on limited samples and strongly non-stationary load series, this study proposes a multi-scale graph–temporal framework for building energy consumption prediction under future climate scenarios. This study builds on conventional data-driven building energy prediction models by introducing multi-scale signal decomposition to process raw building load series. A hybrid model combining a feature-level graph neural network and a bidirectional long short-term memory network is then used to model load components at different frequency scales. This design allows the framework to support future climate scenario analysis, rather than being limited to historical short-term prediction or simulation-derived proxy samples. Based on this hybrid model, an empirical energy–weather relationship is constructed for scenario-based projection. Correction terms are then formulated from simplified thermodynamic mechanisms and operation-strategy settings, and are added to project hourly building electricity loads under future climate scenarios. Building data from different functional types were used together with weather data under different climate scenarios to demonstrate the proposed workflow. The results show that the proposed framework can represent complex fluctuations and non-stationary features in building load series. Historical-stage evaluation across aggregate, transition, ramp, and peak-oriented measures showed comparable overall accuracy to the strongest decomposition-enhanced baseline, with clearer gains during morning and evening load transitions and daily peak prediction. Under the given future meteorological scenarios, the framework can further characterize building-specific changes in typical daily load profiles, annual and seasonal energy consumption, and peak load indicators. Therefore, the proposed method provides an implementable workflow for building energy scenario analysis under future climate conditions.

title: Zero-shot facade parsing for generating building energy modeling inputs using vision-language models and generative image editing
abstract: Building energy modeling (BEM) is a key instrument for assessing energy demand and CO 2 emissions of the building stock and for planning decarbonization strategies. Its reliability, however, critically depends on accurate geometric and material input data, including facade-related parameters such as window areas and window-to-wall ratios that strongly affect solar gains and transmission losses. These facade components can be extracted from images, but current approaches are dominated by supervised deep learning models, which require large annotated datasets, generalize poorly across cities and architectural styles, and struggle with real-world occlusions from vegetation and street furniture. To address these limitations, we propose a zero-shot semantic segmentation workflow with integrated occlusion compensation. The segmentation stage is based on a vision-language model (VLM), and the occlusion compensation stage uses a generative image editing model. Both stages are controlled purely via text prompts and do not require any task-specific fine-tuning. We systematically analyze prompt designs and evaluate the workflow across six facade datasets, including a newly introduced Lemgo Musicians’ Quarter (LMQ) dataset of 92 detached and multi-family residential buildings with pixel-accurate annotations. The experiments show that a unified vision-language-mask model (SAM 3) combined with a flow-matching generative model (FLUX.1 Kontext) achieves the best overall performance: generative occlusion compensation improves Mean IoU on LMQ from 0.760 to 0.801. The downstream analysis shows that occlusion compensation is particularly beneficial for building-area estimation, while its effect on WWR is smaller but removes a systematic overestimation; minor window hallucinations remain a relevant limitation. In cross-dataset evaluation SAM 3 achieves the highest Mean IoU of 0.602, outperforming the strongest per-dataset-trained supervised baseline by approximately 8.6 percentage points, and remaining competitive even against supervised baselines trained on the combined data of all six datasets, while performing on par in intra-dataset settings. By enabling accurate, scalable extraction of facade components with minimal reliance on human-annotated training data, the proposed approach helps mitigate a key data bottleneck in BEM and supports more transferable, up-to-date assessments of building energy performance.

title: A change-point model-based inverse surrogate framework for building and operational parameter inference
abstract: Building parameter characterization is essential for energy performance assessment and retrofit planning, but detailed audits and calibrated simulations are difficult to scale across large building portfolios. This study proposes an inverse surrogate modelling framework to infer unknown building and operational parameters, including internal gains, after-hours plug-load operation, ventilation rate, after-hours ventilation, heating and cooling setback temperature offset, solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) and effective envelope performance (U eff ), from the change-point model (CPM) features extracted from heating and cooling loads. Physics-based simulations were used to generate datasets for four building archetypes across four Canadian weather files, with three weather files used for model development and one reserved as an entirely unseen climate for generalization testing. For each simulation case, occupied and unoccupied heating and cooling CPMs were fitted, and their balance temperatures, slopes, intercepts, and fit-quality metrics were used as inputs to archetype-specific machine learning models. The trained models achieved strong predictive accuracy on the test set, with R 2 values generally ranging from 0.82 to 0.98 across the seven targets and four archetypes. Internal gains, U eff and temperature offset were among the most accurately predicted parameters, with R 2 values of 0.89–0.98 and CV(RMSE) values mostly below 0.18. When evaluated on the entirely unseen weather file, the models maintained promising generalization performance, with most outputs achieving R 2 values above 0.85. Overall, the proposed framework offers a scalable pathway for rapid virtual audits and portfolio-level building characterization.

title: Non-intrusive HVAC scheduling for PV and comfort optimization: A cross-climate predict-then-optimize pipeline
abstract: As solar generation scales across the grid, the bottleneck for decarbonization shifts from production to consumption and the ability of buildings to adapt their largest loads to match renewable availability. Thermal conditioning accounts for a dominant share of building energy demand, and balancing HVAC load shifting with comfort constraints is further complicated by the absence of dense sensor infrastructure in legacy buildings. This paper presents a climate-agnostic, data-driven predict-then-optimise pipeline for HVAC load shifting that maximizes photovoltaic self-consumption while preserving thermal comfort as quantified by the PMV-PPD index. The framework operates in three stages. First, an unsupervised disaggregation algorithm extracts heating and cooling operational states directly from aggregated smart meter readings, eliminating the need for sub-metering. Second, a regime-aware hybrid forecasting architecture combining Temporal Convolutional Networks, LightGBM, and CNN-LSTM models, predicts indoor temperature and relative humidity at the horizon required for comfort-aware scheduling. Third, a predict-then-optimize scheduling loop couples a MILP-based dispatcher which aligns HVAC operation with photovoltaic generation under soft comfort bounds, with the trained forecasting models, repurposed here as comfort simulators that iteratively detect and repair constraint violations, forming a closed-loop control scheme. The framework is validated on two heterogeneous real-world datasets: a residential energy community in Greece (Mediterranean climate,dual heating-cooling regime) and a commercial office complex in Thailand (tropical climate, cooling-only regime). The hybrid forecaster achieves a Mean Absolute Error below 1°C across both test environments. In the first case, the scheduler improves PV self-consumption by an average of 67% while raising occupant comfort by 13%. In the second case, the framework identifies and corrects thermally aggressive AC profiles, yielding a 10.7% comfort improvement and a 16% reduction in overall HVAC activity.

title: Safe mean-field reinforcement learning for cooperative control of large-scale multi-zone HVAC systems
abstract: Efficient control of HVAC systems is essential for reducing building energy consumption while maintaining indoor environmental quality. However, in multi-zone scenarios, strong thermal coupling among zones, together with interactions among temperature, CO 2 concentration, and humidity, results in highly nonlinear and strongly coupled dynamics, thereby significantly increasing the complexity of control decisions. Furthermore, as the number of zones grows, the joint state–action space expands rapidly, leading to the curse of dimensionality and difficulties in coordinated optimization. Consequently, traditional methods struggle to achieve both scalability and satisfactory control performance. To address these challenges, we develop a dynamic optimization model for multi-zone HVAC systems, where multi-variable coupled control is formulated as a multi-agent decision-making problem, capturing both inter-zone and inter-variable interactions. Building upon this, we propose a Safe Mean-Field TD3 (SMF-TD3) algorithm to enable efficient and scalable cooperative control. Specifically, mean-field theory is introduced to approximate individual interactions via aggregated behaviors, thereby reducing system complexity and enabling scalable decision-making. Meanwhile, to satisfy thermal comfort, air quality, and equipment safety constraints, a Lagrangian-based safe reinforcement learning mechanism is adopted, where constraints are embedded into policy optimization and Lagrange multipliers are adaptively updated to balance performance and constraint satisfaction. Finally, in the seven-day, 12-zone simulation, SMF-TD3 reduces electricity cost by 3.37% relative to CPO and 17.11% relative to MADDPG, and cumulative constraint violations by 75.05% relative to MF-TD3. Across the 12-, 20-, and 30-zone systems, training time is reduced by 52.48%–58.44% relative to MASAC, supporting improved economic performance, constraint satisfaction, and scalability under the tested conditions.

title: An innovative applied holistic analytical tool for prescriptive maintenance in the residential sector
abstract: This paper presents a novel holIstic ANalytical Tool FOr PRescriptive Maintenance (INFORM), designed to enhance the reliability and efficiency of home appliances by integrating AI-driven anomaly detection, and automated prescriptive recommendations. Unlike conventional predictive maintenance approaches that require extensive historical, household-specific data before they can be deployed, INFORM combines an offline, cross-device meta-trained model with real-time power consumption analysis, enabling fault detection from the moment of deployment without requiring pre-collected historical data from the specific household or appliance instance, and is subsequently refined through local retraining as real-time data accumulates. Using Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) combined with an Autoencoder-Convolutional Neural Network (AE-CNN), the proposed framework adapts to various household appliances, ensuring accurate fault diagnosis and targeted intervention strategies. The experiments, conducted on washing machines, dishwashers, and clothes dryers, demonstrate improvements in anomaly detection performance and proactive maintenance support, while an illustrative assumption-based analysis indicates the potential of INFORM to support energy-efficiency improvements and Demand-Side Management. The results highlight the potential of INFORM to transform home appliance maintenance into an adaptive, real-time, and prescriptive approach, with the potential to contribute to sustainability and cost reduction in residential energy management.

title: Uncertainty-aware explainable multi-horizon building load forecasting with reservoir computing
abstract: The European Union (EU) is at a pivotal juncture in its energy policy, driven by global energy transitions and the pressing need to combat climate change. Buildings, which account for approximately 40% of total energy consumption and 36% of carbon dioxide emissions in the EU, represent a critical area for optimization. This study proposes an advanced explainable multi-horizon building demand forecasting framework based on Reservoir Computing (RC), enhanced with Monte Carlo dropout(MCd) to quantify predictive uncertainty and an out-of-distribution (OOD) detection mechanism for robust interval forecast validation. The framework leverages the computational efficiency of RC, combined with probabilistic forecasting techniques, to deliver accurate multi-step energy load predictions across diverse operational conditions. Experimental results demonstrate improved forecast measured by multiple metrics, stable prediction intervals that increase under OOD scenarios, and enhanced reliability compared to baseline models. The integration of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), provides detailed insights into the temporal and contextual drivers of energy demand. Key benefits include improved decision-making for energy managers, enhanced occupant comfort, optimized HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning) operations, and seamless integration of renewable energy sources. This framework aligns with the EU's European Green Deal target of carbon neutrality by 2050, offering a scalable solution for smart building energy management. The methodology also supports regulatory compliance, reduces operational costs, and mitigates risks associated with unpredictable energy demand fluctuations.
